legend: Pathfinding is a task of finding a route between two points. It often appears in many problems. For example, in a GPS navigation software where a driver can query for a suggested route, or in a robot motion planning where it should find a valid sequence of movements to do some tasks, or in a simple maze solver where it should find a valid path from one point to another point. This problem is related to solving a maze.

The maze considered in this problem is in the form of a matrix of integers A%%ZSMJ0%% of N×N%%ZSMJ1%%. The value of each cell is generated from a given array R%%ZSMJ2%% and C%%ZSMJ3%% of N%%ZSMJ4%% integers each. Specifically, the value on the ith%%ZSMJ5%% row and jth%%ZSMJ6%% column, cell (i,j)%%ZSMJ7%%, is equal to Ri+Cj%%ZSMJ8%%. Note that all indexes in this problem are from 1%%ZSMJ9%% to N%%ZSMJ10%%.

A path in this maze is defined as a sequence of cells (r1,c1),(r2,c2),…,(rk,ck)%%ZSMJ11%% such that |ri−ri+1|+|ci−ci+1|=1%%ZSMJ12%% for all 1≤i<k%%ZSMJ13%%. In other words, each adjacent cell differs only by 1%%ZSMJ14%% row or only by 1%%ZSMJ15%% column. An even path in this maze is defined as a path in which all the cells in the path contain only even numbers.

Given a tuple ⟨ra,ca,rb,cb⟩%%ZSMJ16%% as a query, your task is to determine whether there exists an even path from cell (ra,ca)%%ZSMJ17%% to cell (rb,cb)%%ZSMJ18%%. To simplify the problem, it is guaranteed that both cell (ra,ca)%%ZSMJ19%% and cell (rb,cb)%%ZSMJ20%% contain even numbers.

For example, let N=5%%ZSMJ21%%, R={6,2,7,8,3}%%ZSMJ22%%, and C={3,4,8,5,1}%%ZSMJ23%%. The following figure depicts the matrix A%%ZSMJ24%% of 5×5%%ZSMJ25%% which is generated from the given array R%%ZSMJ26%% and C%%ZSMJ27%%.
⟨2,2,1,3⟩%%ZSMJ28%%: There is an even path from cell (2,2)%%ZSMJ29%% to cell (1,3)%%ZSMJ30%%, e.g., (2,2),(2,3),(1,3)%%ZSMJ31%%. Of course, (2,2),(1,2),(1,3)%%ZSMJ32%% is also a valid even path.
⟨4,2,4,3⟩%%ZSMJ33%%: There is an even path from cell (4,2)%%ZSMJ34%% to cell (4,3)%%ZSMJ35%%, namely (4,2),(4,3)%%ZSMJ36%%.

⟨5,1,3,4⟩%%ZSMJ37%%: There is no even path from cell (5,1)%%ZSMJ38%% to cell (3,4)%%ZSMJ39%%. Observe that the only two neighboring cells of (5,1)%%ZSMJ40%% are cell (5,2)%%ZSMJ41%% and cell (4,1)%%ZSMJ42%%, and both of them contain odd numbers (7 and 11, respectively), thus, there cannot be any even path originating from cell (5,1)%%ZSMJ43%%.
input: Input begins with a line containing two integers: N%%ZSMJ44%% Q%%ZSMJ45%% (2≤N≤100000%%ZSMJ46%%; 1≤Q≤100000%%ZSMJ47%%) representing the size of the maze and the number of queries, respectively. The next line contains N%%ZSMJ48%% integers: Ri%%ZSMJ49%% (0≤Ri≤106%%ZSMJ50%%) representing the array R%%ZSMJ51%%. The next line contains N%%ZSMJ52%% integers: Ci%%ZSMJ53%% (0≤Ci≤106%%ZSMJ54%%) representing the array C%%ZSMJ55%%. The next Q%%ZSMJ56%% lines each contains four integers: ra%%ZSMJ57%% ca%%ZSMJ58%% rb%%ZSMJ59%% cb%%ZSMJ60%% (1≤ra,ca,rb,cb≤N%%ZSMJ61%%) representing a query of ⟨ra,ca,rb,cb⟩%%ZSMJ62%%. It is guaranteed that (ra,ca)%%ZSMJ63%% and (rb,cb)%%ZSMJ64%% are two different cells in the maze and both of them contain even numbers.
output: For each query in the same order as input, output in a line a string "YES" (without quotes) or "NO" (without quotes) whether there exists an even path from cell (ra,ca)%%ZSMJ65%% to cell (rb,cb)%%ZSMJ66%%.
